title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI-powered issue triage system was deployed in Cline's GitHub repository with broad execution privileges and no access controls on who could trigger it. The system accepted natural language input from anyone opening a GitHub issue, making it vulnerable to prompt injection attacks that could cause it to execute malicious code. A researcher demonstrated this by crafting an issue title that tricked the AI into running commands that would expose publishing credentials for npm, the Visual Studio Code Marketplace, and OpenVSX.

The failure occurred in the automated release workflow that relied on GitHub Actions caches to store credentials. An attacker could poison these caches to plant malicious files that the nightly build process would execute with full publishing permissions. No human review stood between the AI's decisions and code execution in the production release pipeline. The system was designed to operate without rate-limiting, access controls, or verification that issue content came from authorized sources.

It is not established whether any malicious package updates actually reached users, though evidence suggests someone attempted the attack. The vulnerability persisted for over a month from late December 2025 until public disclosure on February 9, 2026, when Cline removed the AI workflows and rotated credentials within an hour.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability that lasted from late December 2025 through February 9, 2026. The flaw existed in Cline's automated issue triage workflow, which used an AI agent running with broad privileges and allowed anyone with a GitHub account to trigger it. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that by opening an issue with a specially crafted title, an attacker could inject prompts that tricked the AI into running malicious code, potentially allowing access to sensitive publication credentials for the Visual Studio Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM.

The attack worked by exploiting GitHub Actions cache poisoning. An attacker could flood the cache with junk data to force GitHub to delete legitimate entries, then plant poisoned cache files that the nightly release workflow would use. This would give attackers access to credentials that could publish malicious updates to millions of Cline users. Although no confirmed malicious updates occurred, evidence suggests someone attempted exploitation. Cline fixed the vulnerability within an hour of public disclosure on February 9, 2026, removing the AI workflows and rotating credentials. Downstream users are advised to disable auto-updates for Cline until full details are confirmed.
